newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Bank of Italy head sees economy stagnating.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Bank of Italy head sees economy stagnating.

text.p: Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio said on Thursday that the Italian economy was stagnating and warned that the situation would not significantly improve in 1997, despite confident government forecasts of an upturn.
However, in a keynote speech, Fazio predicted that Italy would maintain its impressive trade surplus in the coming years and said inflation was set to continue its downward trend.
Italy's economy has been gradually grinding to a halt since the start of the year, wounded by high interest rates and the slowdown seen in other European trading partners.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi has said gross domestic product (GDP) will grow by 0.8 percent this year and 2.0 percent next, but Fazio disagreed: "Economic growth in 1997 will not be far from the unsatisfactory figure seen this year," he said in a speech to mark the world day of savings.
He urged the government to press ahead with its overhaul of the state's heavily indebted accounts.
"Monetary stability and the re-balancing of public accounts are vital if we are to exit from the current phase of economic stagnation," he said.
He said the government should concentrate its future budget efforts on achieving structural spending cuts, adding that this would help bring interest rates down.

The government last month unveiled its 1997 budget, which is designed to cut a massive 62.5 trillion lire ($42 billion) off next year's projected deficit in a last-gasp bid to ensure Italy is a founder member of Europe's planned single currency.
Debate on the package started on Thursday in the full lower house of parliament.

Much of the budget is built around new revenue-raising schemes, including a one-off 12.5 trillion lire "Euro-tax", and employers' federations have criticised Prodi for largely avoiding a structural overhaul of welfare spending.
Fazio indicated that such a revision was now needed.
"Budgetary adjustments should continue by concentrating on the spending side, aiming at structural reforms which would guarantee a long term re-balancing (of accounts)," he said.
"This is necessary for full participation in the process of the integration and construction of a united Europe," he added.

Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi told the same assembly of politicians, businessmen and bankers that Italy was bringing its public finances into line. "Today the path (to stability) is in its final stages...which makes Italy worthy of taking part in the single currency from the start," he said.

On the inflation front, Fazio was more upbeat. He said he expected consumer prices would rise by less than three percent in the last quarter of the year and hoped that this performance would be bettered in 1997.

Inflation ended last year at 5.8 percent and has fallen sharply in the interceding months, hitting 3.4 percent in September, as domestic consumption barely moved in the face of worries over the economic outlook.
With domestic demand depressed, Italy's industrialists have still kept their export boom alive and Fazio predicted exports would continue to outweigh imports in the foreseeable future.

However he did not see any significant let up in Italy's unemployment problem, with nearly 12 percent of the workforce currently without a job. He said the situation demanded increased investment as well as changes to labour laws.
"In the absence of this, the Italian economy is destined to grow only moderatly and will not be in a position to significantly increase the employment total," he said.
